faqs.question: What is the Xenon Illuminator used for?
faqs.answer: The Xenon Illuminator is a compact, high-intensity broadband light source used for photocatalysis research, photovoltaic device testing, laser flash photolysis monitoring, microscopy illumination, and UV exposure studies.

faqs.question: What wavelength range does the Xenon Illuminator cover?
faqs.answer: It covers 200 to 1100 nm with the full-spectrum UV lamp, or 320 to 1100 nm with the ozone-free lamp option.

faqs.question: How much power does the xenon lamp run at?
faqs.answer: The lamp runs at 300 W, with output continuously adjustable between roughly 180 and 300 W to match your protocol.

faqs.question: What's the difference between the full-spectrum and ozone-free lamp options?
faqs.answer: The full-spectrum UV lamp reaches down to 200 nm, while the ozone-free lamp starts at 320 nm and doesn't generate UV-driven ozone during operation.

faqs.question: Can I control the shutter automatically?
faqs.answer: Yes, the integrated shutter can be operated manually or controlled through a TTL signal for automated experiment sequences.

faqs.question: What beam geometry options are available?
faqs.answer: Focused or parallel beam configurations are both available, letting you match illumination profile to your specific application.

faqs.question: How is the lamp cooled?
faqs.answer: The lamp sits in an air-cooled housing with a built-in fan and exhaust system to manage the heat it generates.

faqs.question: How do I know when the lamp needs replacing?
faqs.answer: A Replace-Lamp warning indicator alerts you when lamp performance has declined, alongside a separate Lamp-On indicator for standard status.

faqs.question: What accessories are available for the Xenon Illuminator?
faqs.answer: Optional accessories include fiber optic adapters for coupling to spectroscopic instruments, filter clips for spectral control, and UV shielding for operator protection.

sections.description: Xenon Illuminator product information: lamp configurations, safety features, and accessory options.

body.text: A 300 W air-cooled ceramic xenon lamp sits at the core, producing broadband light across UV, visible, and near-infrared wavelengths.
Output adjusts continuously between roughly 180 and 300 W, so intensity can be tuned to match the specific demands of an experiment rather than running fixed.
An integrated shutter protects samples from unnecessary exposure, controllable either manually or via TTL signal for automated experiment sequences.
Lamps come in two spectral configurations: full-spectrum UV covering 200 to 1100 nm, or ozone-free covering 320 to 1100 nm, with optional filters available to shape the output further.
Focused or parallel beam geometries let you match illumination profile to your application, whether that's concentrated intensity or an even, collimated field.
The housing stays compact enough for standard benchtop integration, despite the strength of the light source inside it.
Air cooling, via a built-in fan and exhaust system, manages the heat the lamp generates during operation.
Indicator lights give direct feedback on system status, including a Lamp-On indicator and a Replace-Lamp warning when performance has declined.

cards.title: Even illumination across a wider field

paragraphs: Two decisions shape how this system performs in your setup: which spectral range the lamp covers, and how the beam itself is delivered.

A full-spectrum UV lamp reaches down to 200 nm, suited to work that genuinely needs UV coverage at the shorter end of the range. An ozone-free lamp starts at 320 nm instead, removing UV-driven ozone generation from the equation for labs where that matters. Optional filters refine either option further, narrowing output to a specific spectral window. On the beam side, a focused geometry concentrates light for applications like laser flash photolysis monitoring, while a parallel beam spreads illumination evenly across a wider field, useful for photovoltaic testing or broader sample exposure.

sections.title: Safety Features and Accessories
body: Cooling, status monitoring, and optional accessories on the Xenon Illuminator.
Running a high-intensity xenon lamp safely and reliably comes down to managing heat and keeping the operator informed, and both are built into the system directly.

The air-cooled housing, with its built-in fan and exhaust system, keeps lamp-generated heat under control during operation. Two indicator lights handle status communication: a Lamp-On indicator confirms the system is active, and a Replace-Lamp warning alerts you before declining lamp performance becomes a problem in your data. Beyond the base system, optional accessories extend what the illuminator can connect to and how operators stay protected, fiber optic adapters for coupling into spectroscopic instruments, filter clips for spectral control, and UV shielding for added operator safety.
